title: Voices Within the Narrative
text:
In nineteenth-century novels, authors often shifted between narrating events from an outside vantage and slipping into a character's consciousness. This technique, known as free indirect discourse, lets the narrator's voice blend with a character's thoughts without the explicit markers of quotation. Readers therefore experience a character's hesitations and self-deceptions as they unfold, rather than as reported facts.

Critics have noted that the device demands a subtle reader, since the boundary between the narrator's judgment and the character's perception can be deliberately blurred. Jane Austen, for instance, uses it so that her heroines' opinions ring with irony, leaving the reader to decide how far to trust them. The result is an intimacy that a purely external narration could not achieve.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what does free indirect discourse allow?
options: It blends a narrator's voice with a character's thoughts without quotation marks
It replaces the narrator with a character's direct speech
It removes all narration from the story
It requires the author to describe events in the future tense

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what does the device demand of the reader?
options: A subtle reader who can judge how far to trust a character
A reader who is a child or a beginner
No interpretation at all, since the story is fully explained
A reader who skips the narrator's comments

questions.text: Why might a reader find it hard to separate the narrator's judgment from a character's perception?
options: Because the boundary between them is deliberately blurred
Because the narrator never appears anywhere in the story
Because the characters speak only in quoted dialogue
Because the author wrote the novel in a different language

questions.text: What can be inferred about the intimacy the device creates?
options: It brings the reader closer to a character's inner world than external narration allows
It keeps the reader emotionally distant from every character
It is achieved mainly through long descriptions of settings
It depends on the reader already knowing the author's biography

vocabulary.definition: a position from which something can be viewed
to combine smoothly so that the parts are hard to tell apart
delicate or hard to notice, requiring careful attention
a difference between what is said or believed and what is actually meant

paragraph_translations: En las novelas del siglo XIX, los autores solían alternar entre narrar los acontecimientos desde una perspectiva externa y adentrarse en la conciencia de un personaje. Esta técnica, conocida como discurso indirecto libre, permite que la voz del narrador se mezcle con los pensamientos de un personaje sin los marcadores explícitos de las comillas. Por eso, los lectores experimentan las vacilaciones y los autoengaños del personaje a medida que se despliegan, en lugar de recibirlos como hechos relatados.

Los críticos han señalado que el recurso exige un lector sagaz, ya que la frontera entre el juicio del narrador y la percepción del personaje puede difuminarse deliberadamente. Jane Austen, por ejemplo, lo emplea para que las opiniones de sus heroínas suenen irónicas, dejando al lector la tarea de decidir hasta qué punto confiar en ellas. El resultado es una intimidad que una narración puramente externa no podría lograr.
